newsitem.title: DENMARK: Alliance to bounce back in UK gas market-Statoil.
newsitem.headline: Alliance to bounce back in UK gas market-Statoil.

text.p: COPENHAGEN, June 13, Reuter - Norwegian Statoil's British gas trading arm Alliance Gas should bounce back from losses last year with the help of a contract to supply National Power plc, Statoil president Harald Norvik told a news conference on Friday.
Alliance lost money in 1996, he said, because of changes in the way the U.K. market operated, but Norvik expected it to be a big player in an expanding European market.
"It seems to us that Alliance is positioning itself very well and it seems it will get bigger as Norwegian gas penetrates the U.K. market more," he said.
Norway's penetration of the U.K. gas market is set to grow following a resolution shortly before Britain's general election on 1 May of the Frigg pipeline dispute between the two countries.

British refusal to allow Norway to export gas other than from the Frigg field and its satellites, even though production there was declining steeply and left the pipeline with unused capacity, kept deliveries at a minimum.
But now Statoil intends to honour a contract it signed in 1991 to supply National Power, which it has so far ben unable to do.

"The most important thing is to get the 2.1 billion cubic metre a year contract going, if the customer wants it," said Norvik. "We will have to renegotiate many elements - many amendments have already been done, it's like a bookshelf, but it shows that the customer and the supplier are keen to keep the contract as something of value to both."
He added that it is uncertain how great UK demand for Norwegian gas will be in the short term, "but in the mid to long term we will be a very significant supplier, and also to Ireland," he said.
Alliance was originally a joint venture with British Petroluem Plc before Statoil bought out its partner's stake.
"When we saw what was happening in the U.K. we wanted to position ourselves as a long term player. At that time we saw an attractive opportunity to cooperate with BP," Norvik said.
Norvik said there had been a logical relationship as BP had short term gas while Statoil had long term gas.
But the market changed and the two companies had different approaches, Norvik said.
